reason: The sources provide detailed, multi-sourced facts detailing the causes, timeline, trapped crew mechanics, and major NASA redesigns following the Apollo 1 launchpad fire.
story: In January 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee boarded Apollo 1 for a routine launchpad simulation. Because the rocket was unfueled, NASA considered the test non-hazardous. But inside the command module, the cabin was pressurized with pure oxygen at high pressure. As the countdown halted to troubleshoot communications issues, an electrical arc near vulnerable wiring ignited flammable nylon and Velcro inside the cockpit. Within seconds, extreme pressure ruptured the spacecraft's inner wall and filled the cabin with toxic smoke. The astronauts attempted to open the hatch per emergency procedures, but the inward-opening plug door design was impossible to pull open against the overwhelming internal pressure. All three crew members died of asphyxiation. The tragedy grounded crewed Apollo flights for twenty months. NASA completely overhauled spacecraft safety, redesigning the hatch to open outward in seconds, replacing cabin materials, and introducing a safer nitrogen-oxygen launch atmosphere.
angle: During a routine ground test, an inward-opening hatch trapped three Apollo 1 astronauts inside a burning pure-oxygen cabin because rapidly rising pressure sealed the door shut from the inside.

claims.claim: Apollo 1 was planned to be the first crewed test flight of the Apollo spacecraft in low Earth orbit.
The Apollo 1 prime crew consisted of astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee.
On January 27, 1967, a deadly fire broke out inside the command module during a pre-launch countdown simulation test at Launch Complex 34.
The launch pad simulation was considered non-hazardous because the Saturn IB rocket was unfueled.
The spacecraft cabin was pressurized with pure oxygen at a high pressure of 16.7 psi prior to the test.
The countdown test was plagued and delayed by persistent audio communication failures between the crew and ground control.
Frustrated by the audio problems, Grissom asked how they were going to get to the Moon if they could not talk between two or three buildings.
The fire's ignition source was determined to be electrical arcing near the floor equipment bay wiring.
Extensive combustible materials inside the cabin, including Velcro strips and nylon netting, rapidly accelerated the spread of the fire.
Internal cabin pressure rapidly rose to 29 psi, sealing the inward-opening hatch shut and rupturing the spacecraft inner wall.
All three astronauts died of asphyxiation caused by high concentrations of carbon monoxide and toxic smoke.
Crewed Apollo launches were suspended for twenty months while NASA completely overhauled command module safety designs.
NASA redesigned the command module hatch to open outward in under five seconds during an emergency.
NASA replaced the pure oxygen launch atmosphere with a safer mixture of 60 percent oxygen and 40 percent nitrogen at launch.
Apollo 1's backup crew of Wally Schirra, Donn Eisele, and Walter Cunningham flew the first successful crewed Apollo mission on Apollo 7 in October 1968.
The Saturn IB launch rocket originally built for Apollo 1 was later repurposed to launch the uncrewed Apollo 5 lunar module test in January 1968.

disputed: Exact final words spoken over the radio loop: sources document multiple garbled audio interpretations ('They're fighting a bad fire', 'We've got a bad fire', 'I'm reporting a bad fire'); scripts should avoid quoting specific variations as absolute fact.

Wally Schirra's pre-flight warning: popular accounts claim Schirra warned Grissom to get out at the first sign of trouble, which contradicts official investigation reports of backup crew debrief satisfaction; scripts should omit this unverified account.

Post-fire body positions: Deke Slayton's eyewitness account differed from the official board report regarding body placement; scripts should focus on cause of death rather than disputed body positions.
